query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidizing boride-based components to form a stable and adherent oxide scale will significantly improve their resistance to molten aluminum corrosion by acting as a passivation barrier against aluminum infiltration.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based component (e.g., TiB2) with a pristine, untreated surface.
generation.intervention: Controlled high-temperature pre-oxidation process (e.g., at 800–900 °C) to develop a uniform oxide layer (such as TiO2 or Al2O3) on the surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure in molten aluminum at approximately 700 °C under cyclic immersion for up to 500 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, coherent oxide scale that adheres to the boride substrate, preventing direct contact with molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The oxide scale serves as a physical and chemical barrier that impedes aluminum-induced corrosion reactions by limiting the diffusion of corrosive species into the underlying boride matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated components, the pre-oxidized components will exhibit lower mass loss, reduced microstructural degradation, and better retention of mechanical properties after prolonged molten aluminum exposure.
generation.baseline: Uncoated or untreated boride-based components exposed to identical molten aluminum conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected within the temperature range of 650–750 °C and for exposure durations up to 500 hours; performance beyond these conditions may require re-assessment of oxide layer stability.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adhesion and durability of the oxide layer under extreme cyclic thermal conditions remain uncertain, and minor variations in pre-oxidation parameters could affect its protective efficacy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical TiB2-based component samples: one set subjected to controlled pre-oxidation at 800–900 °C to form an oxide scale, and one set left uncoated. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at 700 °C under cyclic immersion conditions for a duration of 500 hours.
measurements: SEM imaging for surface microstructural analysis
XRD for phase identification of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in mass retention, microstructural integrity, or mechanical properties compared to the uncoated controls, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: After performing the corrosion tests, the surface was covered with a thin layer of oxide, which was subjected to SEM analyses, and the results are presented in Figure 9. The surface of both samples was covered with a very thin and transparent layer of oxide due to the chemical reactions during immersion in the corrosive solution. In the case of Sample 2 alloy, the oxide layer was thicker and further blurred the surface microstructure. On the surface of Sample 1, a dendritic microstructure under the oxide layer and some corrosion pits were visible.

The XRD patterns of both coatings after hot corrosion for 60 h are shown in Figure 9. It can be observed that the oxide layer of the coating is mainly composed of Al2O3, Cr2O3, and spinels. The PDF numbers are 26,790, 90,157, and 35,002, respectively. After 60 h of hot etching, the coatings retained an intact form within the crucible, but some black oxide products were found at the bottom of the crucible. Figure 10 shows the surface morphologies of the coatings after 60 h of hot corrosion at 900 °C under Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts. Table 4 shows the EDS analysis of the points that are marked in yellow in Figure 10. From Figure 10a,e, it can be seen that after 60 h of hot corrosion, both coatings were covered by oxides and corrosion products. However, the YHf-EHEA coating had a lower spallation area of oxide scales on its surface compared to the EHEA coating. The energy spectrum analyses in Figure 9f show that the internal alloy experiences severe oxidation additionally, the uncoated specimen has a notably higher oxygen content compared to the coated specimen. The surface hardness of the specimens is further compared before and after oxidation, and Figure 10 shows the comparison of the surface hardness of specimens with and without hafnium coating before and after oxidation. The results indicate the surface hardness of the coated specimen decreased by 145 HV, which decreases from 1612 HV before oxidation to 1467 HV after oxidation, with a reduction of 8.995%; the surface hardness of the uncoated VZrHfNbTa HEA decreased by 883 HV, which decreases from 1534 HV before oxidation to 651 HV after oxidation, with a reduction of 57.562%, and the specimen experiences significant deformation. This can be attributed to the oxidation and pulverization of the VZrHfNbTa HEA. The hardness of the coated specimen changes less, possibly due to the HfC and hafnium in the coating forming a dense HfO2 protective layer after oxidizing and sintering.

Consider the quality of the oxide film. F60 showed a uniform and flat surface, and the oxide layer had no obvious cracking, peeling, or other defects. In the cross-section shown in Figure 8, no defects such as cracks and holes were found. Compared with B60, which was not resistant to oxidation, such as a large loss of Al and surface oxide shedding, it is obvious that the oxide film generated by F60 had better integrity and density. It can better protect the substrate. At the same time, compared with the corrosion results of ADSS alloys under similar conditions [], the oxide film of the F0 alloy in this study after corrosion was thinner, the surface oxide particles were smaller and denser, so the protection was stronger, and the microscopic morphology of the corroded surface was more uniform and flatter.

From the comparative analysis of samples D2 and D2TT in relation to the uncoated sample and the analysis of polarization curves with corrosion kinetic parameters, it can be seen that heat treatment improved the corrosion resistance of the alloy. This analysis of the polarization curves indicated that the protective films of the electrodes had an important influence on the cathodic and anodic reactions of the electrochemical process, and it was noted that the electrodeposited film prevented the attack of corrosive ions (Cl−) on the electrode surface. Furthermore, from this analysis, one can observe that the coated electrodes had better protective properties with an efficiency of 50% in relation to the uncovered electrodes.

frame.system: Boride-based material components (e.g., TiB2 or related borides) used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, initially exposed to molten aluminum and prone to corrosion or degradation in an elevated-temperature molten-aluminum environment.
frame.goal: Increase the material’s resistance to chemical attack and wear when in prolonged contact with molten aluminum, thereby enhancing lifespan and performance in hot-dip aluminum-plating processes.
frame.limitation: Currently, boride-based components may degrade when in direct contact with molten aluminum over extended periods, reducing equipment reliability and service life.

decision.trend: Recent work on high-entropy borides (2022) established their stable crystal structures and robustness in extreme conditions, while follow-up studies (2023) on boronizing high-entropy alloys demonstrated improved wear resistance and hardness through surface boride layers. Although these efforts confirm the potential of boride-based materials for harsh environments, they have not explicitly tackled molten-aluminum corrosion in hot-dip plating, leaving an opportunity for further tailored surface engineering to address this gap.
decision.unsolved: Despite the recognized high-temperature stability of borides, their long-term corrosion behavior in molten aluminum and under cyclic immersion remains insufficiently understood. In particular, it is unclear whether protective surface modifications can maintain their integrity and effectively inhibit aluminum-induced degradation over extended service periods at 650–750 °C.
decision.lever: Form a stable, adherent oxide scale (e.g., by controlled pre-oxidation) on the boride component surface to impede direct contact with molten aluminum.
decision.why: Building on evidence that borides exhibit high-temperature stability (PMC9101925) and that engineered boride layers improve wear and corrosion performance (PMC10221107), the next logical step is to develop a protective oxide interface specifically designed to slow or prevent aluminum infiltration. This oxide scale, grown or deposited at processing temperatures near 800–900 °C, would serve as a passivation barrier, protecting the underlying boride from reaction with molten aluminum. In comparison to an unprotected TiB2-based component, the hypothesis is that the pre-oxidized surface will significantly reduce mass loss and microstructural degradation over 500 hours of cyclic aluminum immersion at 700 °C. The proposed approach can be evaluated by preparing samples with and without the oxide layer, immersing both in molten aluminum under standard hot-dip plating conditions, and measuring weight changes, surface microstructure, and mechanical properties before and after exposure. Should the protected samples show similar or greater corrosion than the uncoated controls, the hypothesis would be falsified.
